source_evidence.anchor: Exercise 2.5.9: 'Poisson, exponential, Pareto and Cauchy distributions are not sub-gaussian'
source_evidence.observation: The exercise states four named distribution-family claims, joined as a list, and applies the negative predicate 'not sub-gaussian' to each. It supplies no random-variable symbols, family parameters, or parameter quantifiers.

A random variable X is called sub-gaussian when it satisfies any of the equivalent properties i-iv in Proposition 2.5.2. The same definition sets the sub-gaussian norm to the infimum of positive t for which E exp(X^2/t^2) is at most 2.

For a random variable X, the source makes equivalent: existence of a Gaussian tail parameter K1>0; square-root moment growth with some K2>0; a local bound on the MGF of X^2 with some K3>0; and E exp(X^2/K4^2) <= 2 for some K4>0.
Mean zero is required only for equivalence with the additional ordinary-MGF property (v); it is not an assumption in the definition through properties (i)-(iv).

conclusions: The distribution named 'Poisson' in the exercise, with its family parameter or parameters left unstated, is not sub-gaussian.
The distribution named 'exponential' in the exercise, with its family parameter or parameters left unstated, is not sub-gaussian.
The distribution named 'Pareto' in the exercise, with its family parameter or parameters left unstated, is not sub-gaussian.
The distribution named 'Cauchy' in the exercise, with its family parameter or parameters left unstated, is not sub-gaussian.
definitions_and_conventions: By Definition 2.5.6, a random variable is sub-gaussian exactly when it satisfies the equivalent properties (i)-(iv) of Proposition 2.5.2.
One equivalent criterion is the existence of K4>0 such that E exp(X^2/K4^2) <= 2.
Other equivalent criteria are a Gaussian upper tail bound with some K1>0, square-root growth of all Lp norms with some K2>0, and the stated local exponential-moment bound for X^2 with some K3>0.
The adjective 'not sub-gaussian' negates membership in this class; it is not a claim that the centered MGF property (v) alone fails.
implicit_context: Although the exercise grammatically names distributions rather than random variables, Definition 2.5.6 defines the property for a random variable X; the claim is therefore understood through a random variable having the named law.
The surrounding section treats real-valued random variables, as witnessed by |X|, powers of X, Lp norms, and exponential moments.
No centering assumption is inherited for the sub-gaussian definition.
The exercise relies on conventional meanings of the four named distribution families but does not locally state their probability mass/density formulas or admissible parameter ranges.

details: All four families named in the list must be covered: Poisson, exponential, Pareto, and Cauchy.
The source presents the same negative sub-gaussian conclusion for each family.
No Poisson intensity, exponential rate or scale, Pareto scale or shape, or Cauchy location or scale is displayed.
No explicit universal or existential quantifier over such parameters appears.
The contract therefore leaves parameter dependence implicit rather than adding a binder not present in the source.
The negative claim is relative to Definition 2.5.6 and hence to the equivalent existence conditions in Proposition 2.5.2.
A valid verification may refute any one of the equivalent properties; the exercise does not prescribe which criterion to use.
The four distribution families are distinct objects and the exercise requires a claim about each; none can stand in for another.
Distribution-law language is transferred to a random variable having that law because sub-gaussianity is defined for random variables.

undebatable_constraints: The selected source is Exercise 2.5.9 on PDF page 16, printed page 27, in the hash-pinned first-edition Chapter 2 PDF.
The conclusion is negative: each named distribution is asserted not to be sub-gaussian.
The four named items are Poisson, exponential, Pareto, and Cauchy; a faithful rendering must not omit any one of them.
The exercise itself introduces no random-variable binder and no numerical distribution-family parameter.
The exercise itself states no quantifier over distribution-family parameters and no explicit nondegeneracy side condition.
Sub-gaussianity is the property of Definition 2.5.6, based on properties (i)-(iv) of Proposition 2.5.2.
Mean zero is not a hypothesis for Definition 2.5.6; it is only the condition under which Proposition 2.5.2 adds equivalence with property (v).

ambiguities.issue: The four distribution names denote parameterized families, but the exercise states neither parameter binders nor quantifier scope.
ambiguities.evidence: Exercise 2.5.9 says only 'Poisson, exponential, Pareto and Cauchy distributions' and displays no intensity, rate, scale, shape, location, or universal/existential language.
ambiguities.impact: A formal statement about every admissible parameter, one fixed but arbitrary parameter, or a chosen standard member makes a classification-relevant choice not explicit in the printed claim. This must be surfaced rather than attributed to the source.

ambiguities.issue: No explicit nondegeneracy or strict-positivity convention accompanies the unstated family parameters.
ambiguities.evidence: The exercise has no side conditions. In particular, it does not say that a Poisson intensity is positive or that any scale parameter is nonzero.
ambiguities.impact: If a convention admits a degenerate endpoint such as Poisson intensity zero, a universal claim including that endpoint is false because a constant random variable is sub-gaussian. Excluding such endpoints is mathematically consequential but must be justified as a family convention, not as printed syntax.

ambiguities.issue: The exercise speaks about distributions while the operative definition speaks about a random variable X.
ambiguities.evidence: Exercise 2.5.9 names distribution laws; Definition 2.5.6 begins with a random variable X.
ambiguities.impact: A formalization must choose how to represent 'has this law' and the underlying probability space. This is normally law-invariant, but conflating a distribution object with a random variable is an object-role mismatch.

ambiguities.issue: The exercise does not select a particular equivalent criterion for proving non-sub-gaussianity.
ambiguities.evidence: Definition 2.5.6 cross-references all equivalent properties (i)-(iv) of Proposition 2.5.2, while Exercise 2.5.9 merely asks to check non-sub-gaussianity.
ambiguities.impact: This does not change the mathematical conclusion, but a formal target that negates only a non-equivalent surrogate or silently adds the mean-zero-only property (v) would not capture the source claim.

contract_plain_english: Exercise 2.5.9 asks for four checks: the Poisson, exponential, Pareto, and Cauchy distributions are each outside the sub-gaussian class defined in Definition 2.5.6. The source leaves the variables and all distribution-family parameters implicit, so this contract does not invent parameter binders or a universal/existential parameter quantifier. It records that omission as an ambiguity, especially because degenerate parameter endpoints can matter.
